summary: Gives an overview of terminology and definitions used for two Information-Centric Networking architectures, Named Data Networking (NDN) and Content-Centric Networking (CCNx). In these, communication works by requesting named content rather than sending to addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: A dictionary of words for networks where you ask for things by name, like asking for a book by title.

questions: what is ndn and ccnx terminology
how are data packets signed in icn
subtitle: Terminology for networks where you ask for data by name instead of by address.

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is a new way to build networks, but its concepts do not map neatly to traditional networking vocabulary. Two major ICN implementations, NDN and CCNx, each use different terms for the same ideas.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC collects the terms and definitions used in Named Data Networking and Content-Centric Networking, organized by category: generic terms, node types, forwarding structures, packet types, naming schemes, and security properties.
tldr.outcome: Researchers and engineers now have a shared vocabulary for discussing ICN architectures and can read papers and specifications from both NDN and CCNx communities.

today: RFC 8793 is an Informational RFC from the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It documents terminology used in NDN and CCNx implementations. ICN remains a research topic and is not deployed in production Internet infrastructure, though experimental deployments exist.

sections.title: A Different Kind of Network
sections.content:
Information-Centric Networking changes how networks work at their core. Instead of addresses (like 192.0.2.1), the network routes by names—human-readable identifiers for data. When a consumer wants something, it sends an Interest packet with the name of the data it wants. Routers forward the Interest toward sources and caches. When data arrives, the network returns a Data packet with the same name and the actual content. Routers can cache data in-flight, and the network delivers from the closest copy, not from a fixed source address.

This changes everything: naming becomes central, addresses become optional, multicast happens naturally, and caching is a core feature. Named Data Networking (NDN) and Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) are two prominent ICN implementations. Each uses slightly different terminology for overlapping concepts. This RFC standardizes the vocabulary used in both.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of "mail to 192.0.2.1", you say "give me the book /library/fiction/romance/title". The network finds the nearest copy, even if a router has it cached.

sections.title: Core ICN Concepts
sections.content:
Request-Reply: ICN communication is stateless at the packet level. A consumer sends an Interest; the network returns matching Data. Only one Data packet answers each Interest (flow balance). This is simpler than connection-oriented protocols.

Data Authenticity and Immutability: Every Data packet carries a cryptographic signature that binds its name to its content. This signature is created by the producer and verified by anyone. Once a Data packet is created, the signature ensures that if either the content or the name changes, the change is detected. Data packets are immutable; versioning is used for updates.

Forwarding State: ICN routers maintain three data structures: a Pending Interest Table (PIT) (records unsatisfied Interests), a Forwarding Information Base (FIB) (routes Interests by name prefix, like longest-prefix-match in IP routing), and a Content Store (CS) (in-network cache). When an Interest arrives, the router checks the CS first, then the PIT, then forwards via the FIB.

Segmentation and Versioning: Large data is split into segments with related names. Versions are handled by including a version number in the name. This allows efficient retrieval and disambiguation of multiple versions.
sections.plainLanguage: Three key ideas: (1) ask for data by name, get one answer; (2) prove the data is authentic with a signature; (3) routers remember what they are looking for, cache what they have seen, and know which way to send Interests.

sections.title: Nodes and Their Roles
sections.content:
ICN Consumer: An entity that generates and sends Interest packets. It can be an application or a node in the network.

ICN Producer: An entity that creates and publishes Data packets. It may also store data (a repository) or serve from memory.

ICN Forwarder: A router that implements stateful forwarding. It maintains the PIT, FIB, and CS, and makes decisions about where to forward Interests using a forwarding strategy. Forwarding strategies can use metrics, heuristics, or other information to choose the best next hop.

ICN Data Node: A node that temporarily carries (stores and forwards) an Interest or Data packet, like a store-and-forward relay.

ICN Interface (or "face"): An abstraction for any connection: physical (Ethernet, Wi-Fi), overlay (IP/UDP tunnel), or local (Unix socket between applications). The same forwarding logic works on all types.
sections.plainLanguage: Four kinds of helpers: those who ask, those who answer, those who route and cache, and those who carry things forward.

sections.title: Names and Naming Schemes
sections.content:
Name: A hierarchical sequence of name components (like a URL path: /example.com/photos/vacation/001). Names are semantically meaningful and application-specific. A Packet ID (implicit digest) is a cryptographic hash of a Data packet's content and can be appended to a name to uniquely identify one version.

Exact Name: The name encoded in a Data packet. Full Name: An exact name with the packet ID appended, which uniquely identifies the packet. Prefix Name: A partial sequence of name components, used for longest-prefix-match forwarding (like routing).

Hierarchical Naming: Names are a sequence of labels without assuming a central authority (unlike DNS). Flat Naming: A degenerate case where the entire name is a single label with no structure.

Segmentation: Splitting large data into chunks with a common prefix and different segment numbers. Versioning: Assigning unique names to different versions of data, typically by adding a version component to the name.
sections.plainLanguage: Names are like book titles on a library shelf: hierarchical (/library/section/title), unique (with a hash), and versioned (edition number).

sections.title: Data Security and Trust
sections.content:
Data-Centric Security: Security properties stay with the Data packet regardless of where it is stored or retrieved (unlike in traditional networks where security is tied to the connection). This enables secure caching and forwarding without additional setup.

Data Integrity: Cryptographic mechanisms (like checksums) ensure content has not been corrupted or deliberately modified in transit.

Data Authenticity: Verification that a Data packet comes from a trusted source. Usually achieved with asymmetric signatures (RSA, ECDSA) but can use symmetric signatures (HMAC) within trusted domains.

Data Confidentiality: Keeping data secret. This has two aspects: content confidentiality (encrypting the payload) and name confidentiality (hiding what data is being requested). Note: NDN and CCNx architectures typically handle confidentiality at the application layer, not the network layer.

Trust Model: A set of rules that define which signatures to trust. Trust is distinct from authenticity: a packet is authentic if its signature is valid, but you may not trust that source for a particular purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: The data itself is locked with a signature so anyone can verify it came from the right person, no matter who carried it.
